initial_requirements: Scientists need a grid-based software environment for conducting biogeochemical modeling with weather observations and remote computing resources. The system should let scientific users manage input data, run surface-weather interpolation and ecosystem simulations, visualize results, and manage generated outputs through a graphical interface. It should support secure, reliable use of distributed computing resources without requiring users to handle the underlying grid infrastructure directly.

topics.topic_content: End-to-end modeling workflow in the graphical environment

slots.value: Manage input data, run surface-weather interpolation and ecosystem simulations, visualize results, and manage generated outputs through a graphical interface; scientists choose the study setup, select inputs, decide whether the output is for analysis or to drive a full ecosystem run, and review results for scientific validity. The system should handle repetitive standardized steps such as preparing inputs, launching the right interpolation or simulation job, moving data to and from compute resources, and translating outputs into something the user can view, while scientists still choose the modeling task, review parameters, and decide whether the result is scientifically acceptable. The system may suggest a reasonable default setup, flag likely issues, fill in known defaults, or reuse a previous setup only when the user explicitly asks for it, but it should not make the scientific choice on its own. Defaults should kick in only when the user is creating a new run from a standard template or has explicitly chosen to reuse a previous configuration. If the system can clearly detect the same study area, same model family, and same kind of data, it can prefill the usual parameters to save time. It should refuse to silently apply a default if the change could affect the science, such as switching seasons, grid resolution, calibration settings, or a different scenario; in those cases the scientist should review and confirm the setup before the run starts.

slots.key: Retention and archival of scientific data
slots.value: Active project data should stay online while it is still in use, then move to an archive when it becomes inactive rather than being deleted right away. Archival should usually be triggerable by a project lead or data steward, not by any user, and the system should also be able to suggest archival after data has been inactive for a while. Data should be eligible once the associated job or project is complete and the results have been reviewed or marked as no longer active. Scientific outputs tied to publication, compliance, or reproducibility should be kept under a special retention flag so they are not archived or purged on the normal schedule, and they may need to remain in a more accessible archive with full provenance. Formal approval before moving those special cases is not yet decided. After go-live, the system should support routine admin handling of archive requests, restoring data that was archived too early, correcting retention settings when a project's status changes, and allowing administrators to update retention rules without software changes when policy shifts. New scientific, publication, or compliance rules should be applicable to existing and future outputs in a controlled way with auditability so changes and reasons are visible. Automatic deletion should be off by default unless there is an approved retention policy in place.

topics.topic_content: Submitting jobs to distributed computing resources

slots.value: Distributed computing resources are part of the normal modeling workflow, but the system should manage only the user-facing connection and job submission flow. It should rely on existing grid or cluster infrastructure for low-level resource handling, so scientists do not need to interact with the underlying middleware directly and the application does not reinvent that layer. If certain models or simulations have special submission rules, queue requirements, or data staging steps, those should be built into the application where needed so users can run them correctly without manual workarounds. Where model-specific requirements are known, the system should enforce them automatically before submission, including checking required input files, selecting the right queue, and staging needed data to the remote environment.

topics.topic_content: Surface-weather interpolation execution behavior

slots.value: Runs should proceed only when inputs are scientifically valid and complete for the model; otherwise they should be stopped if there are missing or out-of-range inputs such as incompatible time periods, bad weather coverage, or unsupported grid resolution. Scientists are responsible for choosing the study setup, selecting the inputs, and deciding whether the output is meant just to support analysis or to drive a full ecosystem run. They also need to review the results and judge whether the run looks scientifically valid, especially when there are choices about station coverage, spatial extent, or scenario parameters. The system should preserve which interpolation method was used, what data version went in, and what time period or grid was applied, and it should make any defaults or automatic steps explicit so users can tell whether a result came from their own settings or from system-chosen values. If the system does any automatic preprocessing, filtering, unit conversion, gap filling, station screening, or file transformation, those steps should be recorded too, along with the exact run configuration and any parameter values the user didn’t explicitly set. It should also preserve which software version ran, what remote resource it used, and any job retries or fallback behavior if those could affect the result. The system should handle preparing inputs, launching the right interpolation or simulation job, moving data to and from compute resources, translating outputs into something the user can view, and integrating with existing specialized external tools rather than replacing them; users should not manually handle grid mechanics or file transfers.

A run counts as successful only if it completes without job failures and produces usable outputs that the scientist can review or export, with basic validation confirming expected files were generated and outputs are not obviously incomplete or corrupted. After the run completes and outputs are assembled, the system should compare results against trusted reference or benchmark results before presenting them as fully trusted. If differences are meaningful but still within a tolerable range, the system should flag them for review but keep the run available. If differences are serious enough to make the run questionable, it should be marked as suspect or failed validation, with a clear warning not to use it as a final result until someone checks it.

slots.value: If a run is canceled before completion, the system should preserve whatever safe intermediate state exists, but it must not automatically continue without scientist review. The scientist can restart from that saved state if it is still valid, but must confirm before proceeding. Restart confirmation can be as simple as the scientist reviewing the preserved inputs and clicking to resume, but it should only be allowed when the system shows the same run context they originally canceled from: same study area, same input set, same model version, and same key parameters. If any of those have changed, or if the saved state is incomplete or expired, the system should require a fresh restart instead of quietly restoring the old state and should clearly explain what changed so the scientist can decide whether to rebuild the run.

slots.key: Run proceed, adjust, or stop conditions
slots.value: Runs should proceed only when inputs are scientifically valid and complete for the model. If inputs are missing or out of range, such as incompatible time periods, bad weather coverage, or unsupported grid resolution, the run should be stopped and reported back rather than forced through. Some issues may allow adjustment, such as resampling data to match the grid or interpolating missing weather observations, as long as the system makes this clear to the user. Additional required inputs may also include calibration files, land cover or vegetation descriptions, and scenario-setting files, but only when the selected model or experiment type calls for them. If those required files are missing for a configuration that needs them, the system should block the run and tell the user what is absent.

slots.value: The interface should stay responsive under normal loads so scientists can keep working without much delay, especially for navigation, editing inputs, and basic result viewing. Under heavier workloads like loading large datasets, running multiple simulations, or rendering dense spatial outputs, it is acceptable for the interface to slow down, batch updates, or show a progress state while it catches up. The interface should not feel frozen or lose the scientist’s place, and even when rendering is deferred the user should still be able to cancel, switch tasks, or continue other work where possible. In-progress actions should keep running unless the scientist explicitly cancels them, and the UI should clearly show that they’re still active. Queued updates should stay in order and be applied once the system catches up, so results don’t appear out of sequence or overwrite newer changes. If something can’t be applied yet, the system should preserve it and tell the user what’s pending rather than silently dropping it. Scientists should always know what has already happened, what is still waiting, and what they can safely do next.

revisions.new_value: The interface should stay responsive even when computation takes a long time on remote resources. Day-to-day tasks like loading data, setting up runs, checking status, and turning results into maps or charts should be the fastest parts of the workflow. Modeling can take minutes or hours if the user gets clear progress updates, and visualization should render quickly enough for users to inspect outputs without long waits between changes. Slower processing is more acceptable in the background than during exploration or scenario comparison.

slots.value: If the grid is completely unavailable, fail the submission immediately with a clear message but keep the job definition saved so the scientist can try again later. If it is only partially reachable, do a short automatic retry but not endless retries. For access errors, fail fast and explain that it is a permissions or credentials issue. A retry should count as successful only if the system can fully verify connectivity and submit the job cleanly, not just get a partial response from the grid. If it can’t reach the scheduler, can’t authenticate, or gets a timeout after a reasonable number of attempts, it should stop and show a clear failure message. Repeated transient errors within a short window should also be treated as failure if the system can’t establish a stable path.

slots.key: Security, authentication, and job submission trust
slots.value: Scientists should authenticate with their own accounts, and access should be limited so they can only submit, view, and manage the jobs and data they’re authorized to use. Before a submission is accepted or sent to the grid, the system should verify that the user has permission for the selected dataset, model, and compute resource. If a job is going to run under a shared service account or against a protected remote resource, the system should also check whatever project-level or resource-level authorization is required there. Anything that fails those checks should be rejected before execution. The system should confirm the user is in the right project, has permission for the resource, and that the service account or credential being used is approved for that purpose. It should reject mismatches up front rather than handing them off to the grid, and maintain an audit trail showing who submitted the job and what resource it was meant to use.

slots.key: Graphical interface actions for data and jobs
slots.value: Manage input data, run modeling tasks, visualize results, and manage generated outputs through a graphical interface; scientists use it to move from raw input data to a defensible model result without bouncing between technical tools. In the workflow they should be able to bring in weather and ecosystem data, set up interpolation or simulation runs, launch them on remote resources, and inspect outputs in the same environment. It should save time, reduce manual handling, support repeating runs and comparing scenarios, and make the workflow consistent, traceable, and easy to use regularly without needing grid expertise. The system should hide grid infrastructure details such as node selection, file staging, and job dispatch so scientists can focus on model inputs and outputs. Advanced users or administrators may optionally choose a target resource or adjust run priorities. The system should handle repetitive, standardizable steps such as preparing inputs, launching the right interpolation or simulation job, moving data to and from compute resources, and translating outputs into something the user can view, while the scientist still chooses the modeling task, reviews parameters, and decides whether the result is scientifically acceptable. Specialized external tools in use should be integrated with rather than completely replaced.

slots.value: Provide scientist-friendly status updates and error messages that indicate whether a run is queued, running, failed, or ready for review; modeling can take minutes or hours as long as the user gets clear progress updates. If a run will take longer than a short interactive wait, the system should hand it off to the backend, show progress, and let the user keep working instead of freezing up. For longer queues or heavier loads, it should warn the user that the job is waiting and give a sense of expected delay if possible; warning should also come when jobs are slow to open results or status updates are delayed. Keep the UI in a normal responsive state as long as the handoff is within the expected submission window and live heartbeat/status updates are arriving from the backend. Warn the user once the handoff exceeds the normal submission time for that environment or heartbeat updates stop. The threshold should be based on observed behavior in that environment rather than a fixed arbitrary number. Queued updates should stay in order and be applied once the system catches up, so results do not appear out of sequence or overwrite newer changes. If something cannot be applied yet, the system should preserve it and tell the user what is pending rather than silently dropping it.

slots.key: Authorization for data and job actions
slots.value: Access should be limited so scientists can only submit, view, and manage the jobs and data they’re authorized to use. Before submission, the system should verify permission for the selected dataset, model, and compute resource; if a job runs under a shared service account or against a protected remote resource, project-level or resource-level authorization must also be checked. For jobs that need a shared service account or protected remote resource, the system should confirm the user is in the right project, has permission for that resource, and that the service account or credential being used is approved for that purpose. If a submission doesn’t match those checks, it should be rejected up front rather than handed off to the grid. An audit trail should record who submitted it and what resource it was meant to use. Access to retained provenance and original run details should still follow project- and role-based permissions; users may be able to see that a run existed and that an output was superseded, but not necessarily view all underlying inputs or resource details unless authorized. For archived or deleted items, visibility should be limited to people with the right project access or admin rights, with more sensitive run details hidden when needed. For related output links, authorized users should reach an archived version directly if it is still available; if not directly accessible, they should at least see a recovery or request path. If a newer related output exists, the system should redirect or clearly point to that version while preserving the trail back to the original run.

slots.key: Remote job workflow and result handling
slots.value: Users should not handle grid infrastructure directly; the system should hide node selection, file staging, and job dispatch so scientists can focus on model inputs and outputs. The system should also handle repetitive workflow steps that are easy to standardize, including preparing inputs, launching the right interpolation or simulation job, moving data to and from compute resources, and translating outputs into something the user can view. Scientists should still choose the modeling task, review parameters, and decide whether the result is scientifically acceptable. For normal scientific use, workflow automation should cover as much grid handling as possible, with grid details surfaced only when something goes wrong or a decision is needed. Advanced users or administrators may optionally choose a target resource or adjust run priorities. Where model-specific requirements are known, the system should automatically enforce them before submission by checking required input files, selecting the right queue, and staging needed data to the remote environment, and it should prevent obvious bad submissions such as missing parameters or using a queue that can’t support the job type. A run should count as successful only if it completes without job failures and produces usable outputs that the scientist can actually review or export; it must also pass basic result validation, such as confirming expected files were generated and outputs are not obviously incomplete or corrupted.

slots.key: Scientist-friendly job status and error messaging
slots.value: Status updates should reflect queued, running, failed, or ready-for-review states; warning signs of approaching normal concurrent workload capacity include slow data uploads, delayed status updates, long waits to open results, and a sluggish GUI while users are managing projects. For heavier loads or longer queues, the system should warn users or provide monitoring so they know when they are nearing the limit. During heavy scientific workload periods, the service should stay usable and not lose work, even if some operations slow down when many runs are happening at once. In-progress actions should keep running unless the scientist explicitly cancels them, with the UI clearly showing they are still active. Queued updates should stay in order and be applied once the system catches up, and anything not yet applicable should be preserved and shown as pending rather than silently dropped.

slots.key: Scientific data retention and archival policy
slots.value: Automatic deletion should remain off by default unless there is an approved retention policy in place. Active project data should remain online while it is still in use, then move to an archive when it becomes inactive rather than being deleted right away. Archival should usually be triggerable by a project lead or data steward, not just any user, and the system should also be able to suggest archiving when data has been inactive for a while. Data becomes eligible for archival once the associated job or project is complete and the results have been reviewed or marked as no longer active. Outputs tied to publication, compliance, or reproducibility should carry a special retention flag so they are not archived or purged on the normal schedule and may need to remain in a more accessible archive with full provenance. Formal approval before moving those special cases is not yet decided. After go-live, the system should support routine admin handling of archive requests, restoring data that was archived too early, correcting retention settings when a project’s status changes, and letting administrators update retention rules without changing the software. If new scientific, publication, or compliance rules come in later, the platform should be able to apply them to existing and future outputs in a controlled way with auditability for what changed and why. Keep run provenance even if the output itself is deleted or moved to archive, including the original run ID, inputs, timestamps, and who executed it. If an output is superseded, clearly mark that relationship and point to the newer run or output version. Provide links to related outputs and any archived location or recovery path where applicable so results can be traced later for comparison or publication.
